title: E34 - How Will AI Work with Document Management? NetDocuments CPO Dan Hauck
author: Dan Hauck

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s central claim that automation may erode apprenticeship and verification capacity. Instead, it reframes AI as an on-demand training and case-familiarisation aid that can improve continuity of client service. Its support is anecdotal and does not establish whether AI-assisted learning reproduces durable expertise.
qs: You know, today, I think about like how much better I would have been trained had I been able to just ask an AI, like, hey, partner is asking me to do this.
And so I say, it's not even about billable time, it's about providing great client service.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that practical legal AI depends on workflow-specific configuration and organisational context. It materially extends that proposition with concrete document-ingestion examples—custom extraction, metadata enrichment, security classification and retention rules—while offering product descriptions rather than measured reliability evidence.
qs: So, it's really designed to be able to adapt to the workflow that the law firm has or that the organization has.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of AI as a tool for developing expertise rather than merely replacing labour, and materially extends it by identifying everyday assistants as sources of assignment guidance, precedent discovery, case orientation and informal feedback when colleagues are unavailable. Its contribution is qualitative and retrospective, so it does not establish improved training outcomes.
qs: You know, today, I think about like how much better I would have been trained had I been able to just ask an AI, like, hey, partner is asking me to do this.

And I think that's where it's just been so important to help lawyers recognize how it can be, you know, that assistant that can be there to bounce ideas off, to ask questions, to validate some of your ideas.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-specific, workflow-embedded model and materially extends it with concrete document-management applications: bounded classification and metadata extraction using smaller models at repository scale, supported by advance data preparation and integration into existing workflows. Its evidence is mainly vendor demonstrations and customer feedback, however, and does not substantively address verification or independent outcome evaluation.
qs: But when you're talking about a classification scenario, it's a much more straightforward analysis where you have a list of document types, for instance, from a taxonomy, you have a document and you say which one is the best match for this.

So to be able to show that, again, not just as this is where we're going and this is how it's going to work, but this is in the world and we have netters who are doing this right now at scale across millions of documents.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of agentic AI as tool-enabled orchestration rather than a standalone chatbot, illustrating this with document-management search, editing and extraction capabilities. Its claim that tool use may mitigate hallucinations is predictive and unsupported by measured reliability evidence, so it does not resolve the cluster’s concerns about error propagation or verification bottlenecks.
qs: What we were able to do was take a really strong agentic architecture model that now has access to tools, like the editing tool I talked about before.

And I think, to me, I think this is going to end up being like one of the most significant, like, advances in AI when people realize that there's a lot of tools that we use both in the real and the digital world that mitigate against hallucination.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster by looking beyond AI branding to core document management and lawyer-specific working practices. Its product positioning is consistent with user-led implementation, but it provides no technical detail or measured evidence that the differentiated co-authoring approach improves outcomes.
qs: We spent a lot of time actually today talking about, you know, the things that we're doing in core document management with Microsoft and doing fun things like co-authoring and how we're doing co-authoring differently than how other folks are doing it, because we recognize the way lawyers work is special and different.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s claim that corporate legal departments are independent and sometimes comparatively advanced AI customers. Its evidence is qualified and anecdotal, however, and does not establish selective insourcing, stronger buyer power or reduced outside-counsel spending.
qs: I think one of the surprises that I've seen both in industry surveys and anecdotally is that actually in-house council are in some cases using AI significantly more than their law firms.
They're using NetDocuments just as a law firm might, in order to track all the different matters that they have kind of going on.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view of AI as a bounded assistant that improves legal production rather than autonomously replacing lawyers. Its document-grounded matter familiarisation and continuity examples show practical context assembly, while its emphasis on client service over billable-time reduction reinforces augmentation and workflow improvement. The reported faster in-house adoption is directionally consistent with buyer-side reallocation, though it is only weakly substantiated.
qs: And what we're seeing now is people who are, you know, they have all that content loaded in the documents, and they just ask the assistant, hey, here's these 25 depositions.
And so I say, it's not even about billable time, it's about providing great client service.

kp.k: AI adoption is moving beyond experimental deployments
kp.d: Dan Hauck reports that NetDocuments' Assistant had been in market for over a year and customers had established implementation, adoption and training programmes. He describes customer surveys and practice-group feedback as informing product development, and later reports repeated daily and weekly use. These are vendor-reported adoption observations; the transcript supplies no survey sample sizes or utilisation figures.
qs: we've had some of our AI products like our Assistant in market now for over a year, and there have been implementation and adoption and training programs that have been put in place.
We're seeing lawyers returning week after week, day after day, starting to use the assistant and that stickiness of the assistant as part of that workflow.

kp.d: Hauck contrasts the previous year's targeted matter applications, such as due diligence, with an ingestion pipeline designed to classify every saved document and extract metadata. He claims capacity for hundreds of millions of documents, reports current deployment across millions, and says tens of thousands can be processed in minutes. These are product capability and deployment claims, not independently documented performance results.
qs: every document, hundreds of millions of documents can now be profiled with AI profiling.
over the past year, we've been developing our technologies so that we can apply this as part of an ingestion pipeline so that you can actually do it to every document.
We're able to do this across tens of thousands of documents in a matter of minutes.

kp.k: Curated taxonomies reduce customer implementation work
kp.d: Hauck says customers want trusted classifications and data fields without constructing their own taxonomy or consulting every practice group. NetDocuments supplies a pre-built taxonomy developed with knowledge-management experts and informed by existing classification solutions. He presents this standardisation as a complement to the technical pipeline that makes repository-wide profiling achievable.
qs: They don't want to have to figure that out themselves.
we actually worked with leading experts who've been working in knowledge management for a very long time
Do I need to go to every single practice group and ask what kind of documents they work on and what pieces of data they have to get? No, you can use a very well-curated taxonomy.

kp.k: Smaller models enable economical classification at scale
kp.d: Hauck attributes scalability partly to newer lightweight, cost-effective models, naming GPT-5 Nano and GPT-41 Mini as transcribed. He distinguishes relatively straightforward taxonomy matching and extraction from token-intensive reasoning tasks. He claims smaller models outperform earlier brittle machine-learning approaches requiring extensive training examples, but gives no accuracy measurements. He also identifies earlier models' speed, accuracy and context-window limitations as obstacles that have diminished.
qs: Things like GPT-5 Nano and GPT-41 Mini, which can provide a lot of these classifications at scale.

when you're talking about a classification scenario, it's a much more straightforward analysis where you have a list of document types, for instance, from a taxonomy, you have a document and you say which one is the best match for this.
much better than what we saw from kind of prior machine learning type of solutions that had were very brittle, required a lot of training, a lot of sample documents to get through.

kp.k: Custom ingestion workflows extend classification into governance
kp.d: Hauck describes configurable workflows for specialised documents and extraction requirements, with stronger models available for more complex subsets. He reports customers adding summaries, identifying personally identifiable or protected health information to support security policies, and applying organisation-specific retention policies. NetDocuments' professional services team supports this customisation alongside its standard offering.
qs: you might find that you want a more high-powered model to hit those subset of documents in order to address really more complex questions.
They want to classify it, whether or not it has PII or not, or PHI, so that they can apply the right security policies and things like that.
they might have certain retention policies that are unique to them that they want to be able to apply in this ingestion pipeline.

kp.k: Document management expands into substantive editing workflows
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz frames richer classification as potentially extending document management beyond precedent retrieval into repapering, due diligence and discovery. Hauck specifically illustrates contract repapering: extracted metadata identifies the relevant documents, and an Assistant editing tool modifies document XML rather than depending on an open Word session. He describes batch instructions across 100 documents and newly versioned outputs, while also describing lawyers accepting or modifying suggested redlines.
qs: just like an associate giving you a red line, you can then go through it and accept those suggestions or modify them.
Actually all of the operation is happening under the hood in the XML of the document.
without ever having to open up Microsoft Word 100 times, you're going to have newly versioned edited documents according to your instructions.

kp.k: Agentic search automates iterative document investigation
kp.d: Hauck says NetDocuments invested in agentic architecture rather than a straightforward chatbot, giving its Assistant search and editing tools and an extraction tool being made available that year. He describes repeated searches, document retrieval and adjustments to locate answers, including reconstructing a board-membership timeline with linked citations. Abramowitz separately argues that tool use can mitigate hallucination by analogy with human measurement tools; no measured reduction in hallucinations is provided.
qs: we invested heavily in our agentic architecture.
it being able to conduct not just one search, but dozens of searches in order to quickly then evaluate the content, fetch that document or set of documents, and look for the answer inside of it
all of the answers are then cited and linked back to the content that it used inside of NetDocuments.

kp.k: Software consolidation offers a concrete ROI argument
kp.d: Hauck reports customer case studies in which AI workflow applications replace separate tools, enabling six-figure software-spend savings through consolidation onto NetDocuments. He distinguishes this relatively straightforward ROI story from emerging fixed-price opportunities for repetitive work at scale where users are confident in results. He says those pricing applications remain in development and, reporting Nikki's observation, distinguishes isolated examples from a market-wide shift.
qs: we actually have saved six figures on our software spend by consolidating our AI onto NetDocuments.

There are obviously some of the scaled use cases of being able to do certain work at scale that's repetitive, or that you feel confident in terms of the results, that then you can start giving fixed prices to your clients on.
We're still waiting to see the entire market start to shift towards that, but you can find those as well.

kp.k: Assistant value includes enjoyment and intellectual support
kp.d: Hauck says the value of convenient, secure assistance remains difficult to quantify and emphasises attorney experience. He gives a personal example of asking AI what he had missed after reviewing a contract. Abramowitz endorses this augmentation model—lawyers doing their work before asking AI to review or challenge it—and speculates that post-pandemic isolation helped drive adoption because AI provides a sounding board. These experiential claims are not quantified productivity or wellbeing findings.
qs: we're still working on ways that we can capture what that value is. But attorney happiness matters.
I basically said, you know, what am I missing here? What are the things that I need to be thinking about that I haven't thought about before?
do your work and then ask the AI to like review, help you think about like what you might have missed in that example.
I think that part of what AI did was it relieved some of that loneliness.

kp.k: AI supports associate learning and matter onboarding
kp.d: Abramowitz retrospectively suggests an AI tutor could have helped him understand unfamiliar assignments and locate precedents as an associate. Hauck reports customers using the Assistant to summarise participants across 25 depositions and then investigate individual testimony. They frame this as helping lawyers taking over matters acquire context more quickly, including after departures or leave; Hauck emphasises client service rather than billable-time savings. No measured training or onboarding outcomes are supplied.
qs: today, I think about like how much better I would have been trained had I been able to just ask an AI
hey, here's these 25 depositions. Help me understand, you know, give me a summary of who these people are.
it's not even about billable time, it's about providing great client service.

kp.k: In-house incentives and AI-equipped clients pressure outside counsel
kp.d: Abramowitz says unspecified industry surveys and anecdotes suggest in-house counsel sometimes use AI significantly more than outside counsel, contrary to his expectations. Hauck explains corporate uptake through cost management and the absence of billable-hour tensions. He also relays a conversation about clients using generative AI to interrogate lawyers' work product, likening this to patients arriving with WebMD-informed questions, and argues firms increasingly see AI as part of client-service delivery. The transcript offers no comparative adoption statistics.
qs: one of the surprises that I've seen both in industry surveys and anecdotally is that actually in-house council are in some cases using AI significantly more than their law firms.
They don't have that tension with the billable hour and reduced work and so forth.
it actually reminded me a bit of when WebMD became, you know, so popular and people were showing up at their doctor and saying, you know, what about this and that sort of thing.
the law firms are recognizing that, you know, this is going to be part of great client services delivery kind of going forward.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dan Hauck describes AI turning document management into a platform for repository-wide classification, legal workflows, agentic search and lawyer assistance.
pts.d: Hauck claims NetDocuments can now classify documents and extract metadata at repository scale using lightweight models, which he describes as faster and more accurate than earlier machine-learning solutions. Custom ingestion workflows can add summaries, identify sensitive information and support security or retention policies. He says integrated classification and document-level editing allow lawyers to identify contracts for repapering and apply edits across multiple documents without opening each in Word; lawyers can accept or modify suggested redlines. He describes an agentic assistant that conducts repeated searches, retrieves documents and produces answers linked to source content. He also claims platform consolidation can reduce software spending, and reliable repetitive workflows can support fixed client prices, although that pricing shift remains developing. He reports assistants becoming embedded in lawyers' daily work, supporting idea testing and faster familiarisation with matters. For corporate legal departments, he identifies cost management and the absence of billable-hour tensions as adoption incentives. He anticipates AI becoming part of law firms' client-service delivery. These are Hauck's claims as the interviewed product executive, rather than independently established findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Hauck relies on product development experience, conference demonstrations, customer feedback, reported case studies and personal use; he supplies no detailed benchmark results.
pts.d: For adoption, Hauck cites customer implementation and training programmes, utilisation surveys, practice-group feedback and repeated assistant use, without reporting sample sizes or usage rates. For classification, he cites internal testing, a pipeline developed over the preceding year, a taxonomy informed by knowledge-management experts and existing taxonomies, demonstrations, and activity across millions of documents. His stated throughput is tens of thousands of documents in minutes, but he provides no test protocol, accuracy percentages or comparative measurements supporting the claimed superiority to earlier systems. For financial ROI, he reports customer case studies of consolidation and six-figure software savings, without identifying customers or providing calculations. He explicitly says the value of the assistant experience is still difficult to capture. He supplies a personal contract-review example for AI as a sounding board. His observations about corporate incentives are interpretive; the account of clients questioning AI-reviewed work product is a second-hand anecdote, not a measured market finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most capabilities are presented as current at the interview; some tool availability and broader pricing changes remain prospective or conditional.
pts.d: In this source labelled 2025, Hauck says the Assistant has been in market for over a year and distinguishes the previous year's targeted projects from current ingestion-pipeline classification. He attributes current scalability to improvements in model speed, accuracy, context windows and cost. Straightforward classification uses a predefined taxonomy and smaller models; specialised documents may require customisation, professional-services support or a more powerful model. Repapering depends on proper classification and extraction to identify the relevant documents, while suggested edits remain subject to user acceptance or modification. Agentic search is described as available, whereas an extraction tool is described as becoming available 'this year', without a specific date. Fixed pricing is conditional on repetitive work and confidence in results and remains an emerging use rather than a market-wide transition. Habitual assistant use is described as occurring after users reach a level of engagement, not automatically upon deployment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern law firms, corporate legal departments, knowledge-management teams, individual lawyers and their clients.
pts.d: For firms and organisational knowledge-management teams, Hauck describes reduced work defining classifications practice group by practice group and broader reuse of repository content. For transactional lawyers, integrated classification and editing support bulk contract changes; for litigators and lawyers joining ongoing matters, summaries and question-answering over depositions help them acquire context faster. For individual lawyers, the assistant takes on time-consuming searching and provides a sounding board, while retaining a human role in reviewing proposed edits and exercising judgment. For provider organisations buying software, consolidation offers claimed licence-spend savings. For corporate legal departments, including customers with hundreds of lawyers, spend-management incentives favour adoption without the same billable-hour tension. For clients, Hauck frames faster lawyer onboarding and greater focus on substantive work as service benefits, with fixed pricing a developing possibility. The source does not offer concrete predictions about lawyer headcount, entry-level displacement or access to justice.
